paras: The lynching of A. Brown (Sam Miller) was the hanging of a Black man by a party of men who took him from the jail at Newnan, Georgia, on the night of August 9, 1882. He had been accused of outraging a fifteen-year-old white girl in Campbell County and brought to Newnan for safe keeping. An Atlanta dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several papers printed it under headings approving the killing.

According to the Atlanta dispatch as printed in Savannah, the man came from Campbell County and was accused of outraging a fifteen-year-old white girl. He had been carried to Newnan, where he was held in jail for safe keeping. A separate brief instead said the charge was an attempt to outrage a white woman in Campbell County.

On the night of Wednesday, August 9, a party of men took him out of the Newnan jail. The dispatch put the party at seventy-five men, while the Sam Miller brief described seventy masked men. The dispatch said he was 'tried' by the crowd and confessed that he and another man had committed the deed, a claim it did not attribute to any source. He was then hanged; the Savannah Morning News headline placed the hanging near Newnan, and no account describes the spot.

The other man said to have been implicated was never named in the coverage, and no report of his arrest appears. No report of an inquest, arrests of the lynchers or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The story spread chiefly through one Atlanta dispatch dated August 10, which appeared that day in Yankton and on August 11 in New York, Washington, Savannah, Las Vegas and Salt Lake City. Shorter digests followed in news roundups through late August, including the Weekly Clarion of Jackson, Mississippi, and the Abbeville Press and Banner. Many printings left the man unnamed, while the Savannah Morning News and the Marietta Journal called him A. Brown and a Kentucky and an Ohio weekly called him Sam Miller.

Headlines framed the killing as deserved punishment. The Savannah Morning News headlined 'A Negro Fiend Hanged Near Newnan,' the National Republican of Washington ran the dispatch as 'Served the Scoundrel Right,' the Salt Lake Herald as 'His Deserts,' and the Tombstone Epitaph as 'Proper Treatment.' Other papers used plainer heads such as 'A Negro Lynched by a Mob' or 'Hung by a Mob', but nearly all repeated the crowd's claimed confession as fact.

The reports disagree on the man's name, giving A. Brown, Aleck Brown and Sam Miller, though all describe a single man taken from the Newnan jail on a Campbell County accusation. The size of the party is given as seventy-five in the main dispatch, seventy in the Miller brief, and fifteen in two western copies of the dispatch. The Cheyenne Daily Leader dated the seizure to Thursday night, but the dispatch dated August 10 and the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier both point to Wednesday, August 9.

reader.title: Lynching of A. Brown (Sam Miller)
bases: A Black man accused of outraging a white girl was taken from the jail at Newnan by a party of seventy or seventy-five men and hanged (A5, A22, A25).

Every account says the man was taken out of jail and hanged by a party of men (15, 70 or 75 by different versions) with no legal process, after a crowd 'trial' on an accusation of outraging a white girl (A5, A20, A22). The crowd's 'trial' and the claimed confession present the killing as punishment for an alleged crime (A1, A5).

Most items reprint one August 10 Atlanta dispatch (A1, A5, A6), but a separately worded brief naming Sam Miller and describing seventy masked men (A22, A24) and a Georgia weekly (A25) agree on the core event of a jail seizure and hanging at Newnan.

accounts.gist: A Black man from Campbell County, accused of outraging a fifteen-year-old white girl and carried to Newnan for safe keeping, was taken out of jail at night and hung by seventy-five men after the crowd 'tried' him and, it said, he confessed with another man.

framing.detail: Savannah headlined 'A Negro Fiend Hanged Near Newnan'; the National Republican ran the dispatch as 'Served the Scoundrel Right', the Salt Lake Herald as 'His Deserts', the Tombstone Epitaph as 'Proper Treatment'.
Most papers printed the Atlanta dispatch or a one-line digest under neutral heads such as 'A Negro Lynched' or 'Hung by a Mob', repeating the claimed confession as fact.

conflicts.note: All versions describe one man taken from the Newnan jail on a Campbell County accusation; none reports two men hanged. The Georgia papers' 'A. Brown' is the better-sourced name.

versions.value: Wednesday night / 'last night' in an August 10 dispatch (August 9)

conflicts.note: The dispatch dated August 10 and published that day fixes the night as August 9; Thursday appears only in a later digest.
The Georgia papers spell Newnan; 'Atlanta' appears to be the dispatch dateline taken for the site.
The fifteen figure appears only in two western copies of the same dispatch, likely a transmission error for seventy-five.
